intro.html: Some explanations make you nod; others make you squint. These words describe ideas, directions and writing on both sides of that line. Several began as words about light: lucid and elucidate hold Latin lux (light), while opaque and obscure first meant dark or shaded.

Clear: lucid, coherent (holds together), explicit (stated outright), incisive (sharp, to the point); to make clear is to elucidate. Unstated: implicit (suggested, not said). Unclear: opaque, obscure, nebulous (hazy), convoluted (twisted and tangled).

words.ex: Ada gave a {lucid} explanation of how rainbows form.
words.ctx: The instruction booklet was a jumble of tiny print, but Grandpa’s note was {lucid}: three short steps, each with a simple drawing.
words.etym: From Latin lucidus, “bright, clear,” from lux (light).

mn.cue: LUCY-d: Lucy’s map is CLEAR as day
mn.text: Lucy’s map is so clear that anyone can follow it: one big arrow, three landmarks and an X. Her map is {lucid}.

scene.alt: A girl named Lucy holds up a clear, simple map, and a boy happily points the way.

words.def: logical and consistent; holding together clearly
words.ex: After a good night’s sleep, Dev rewrote his messy essay until it was finally {coherent}.
words.ctx: Lila’s story was {coherent} from start to finish: each event led to the next, and the ending tied every loose thread together.
words.etym: From Latin cohaerere, “to stick together”: co (together) + haerere (to stick).

mn.text: Every piece of Pip’s puzzle fits and sticks to the next, making one clear picture. Like his puzzle, his story is {coherent}.

scene.alt: A boy cheers beside a table where his puzzle pieces fit neatly together.

words.def: stated clearly and fully, leaving nothing to guess
words.ex: Mom’s rules were {explicit}: homework first, then one hour of games.
words.ctx: The sign was {explicit}, “No dogs on the beach from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., no exceptions,” so no one could claim to have misunderstood.
words.etym: From Latin explicitus, “unfolded, laid out,” from explicare: ex (out) + plicare (to fold).

mn.text: The beach sign spells it out in big letters, NO DOGS!, so Ivy and her pup turn around. The rule is {explicit}.

scene.alt: A girl and her dog stop in front of a large beach sign that says No Dogs.

words.ex: Her smile carried an {implicit} invitation to join the game.
words.ctx: No one said that the new kid could sit with them, but the invitation was {implicit} when Maya scooted over and patted the empty spot on the bench.
words.etym: From Latin implicitus, “folded in, entwined,” from implicare: in (in) + plicare (to fold).
words.note: Implicit means unstated, not “hidden on purpose.” It can also mean complete and unquestioning: implicit trust.

mn.text: Maya never says “Sit with me,” but she scoots over and pats the bench. The invitation is {implicit}.

scene.alt: A teen on a bench smiles and makes room for a shy boy holding his lunch, inviting him without a word.

words.def: sharp and direct; going straight to the heart of the matter
words.ex: The coach’s {incisive} comment fixed Kai’s swing in a single sentence.
words.ctx: While the others rambled about the lunch menu, Rosa asked one {incisive} question, “Who is paying for it?”, and the whole debate came to a halt.
words.etym: From Latin incisus, “cut into,” from incidere: in (into) + caedere (to cut).

mn.cue: IN-CIS-ive: CUTS right IN to the point
mn.text: The meeting is a tangle of talk until Rosa’s one sharp question cuts straight through it, like an arrow. She is {incisive}.

scene.alt: A teen asks one sharp question that cuts through a tangle of talk, and two men look surprised.

words.ex: The museum guide {elucidated} how the ancient water clock kept time.
words.ctx: Seeing the puzzled faces, the teacher paused to {elucidate}: she drew a diagram, gave two simple examples and then had the class try one together.
words.etym: From Late Latin elucidare, “to make clear”: e (out) + lucidus (bright, clear).

mn.cue: E-LUC-idate: bring it OUT into the LIGHT
mn.text: Professor Edwin draws a simple picture on the board, and one by one the puzzled faces light up: “Oh, I see!” He {elucidates} the idea.

scene.alt: An old professor explains at the blackboard, and his students' faces light up with understanding.

words.def: hard to understand; also, not letting light through
words.ex: The {opaque} curtains kept the bedroom dark even at noon.
words.ctx: The notice was so {opaque}, full of long words and endless sentences, that Dad had to call a lawyer just to find out what it meant.

mn.cue: oh-PAQUE: a box on your head: no seeing through
mn.text: For the costume party, Dev wears a cardboard box over his head. No light gets through; he can’t see out, and no one can see in. The box is {opaque}.

scene.alt: A teen with a cardboard box over his head gropes about, unable to see, while a woman laughs.

words.def: not clear or easy to understand; also, not well known
words.ex: The joke was too {obscure} for anyone at the table to get.
words.ctx: The song was written by an {obscure} composer whom few people had ever heard of, yet once the radio played it, the whole town was humming along.
words.note: Obscure has two senses: hard to understand (an obscure poem) and little known (an obscure village). As a verb, to obscure is to hide from view.

mn.cue: ob-SCURE: so dim, no one is SURE
mn.text: Through the thick fog, Sven can barely make out a shape on the water: a boat? a whale? No one is sure. It is {obscure}.

scene.alt: A man on the dock squints into thick fog, unsure what shape is out on the water.

words.def: vague and unclear in form or meaning; hazy
words.ex: Kai had only a {nebulous} plan for the weekend: “do something fun.”
words.ctx: The club president’s promises were {nebulous}, all “better days ahead” and “a brighter future,” with no details about what she would actually do.
words.etym: From Latin nebulosus, “misty, cloudy,” from nebula, “mist, cloud.”

mn.text: Ask Jonah what his new invention does, and his answer is as fuzzy as a cloud: “It… sort of… does stuff?” His idea is {nebulous}.

scene.alt: A teen shrugs, unsure what his invention does, while his idea floats in a fuzzy cloud.

words.def: so twisted and complicated that it is hard to follow
words.ex: The directions to the cabin were so {convoluted} that we got lost twice.
words.ctx: The movie’s plot was {convoluted}: twins swapped places, a villain turned out to be a hero, and three different maps led to the same treasure.
words.etym: From Latin convolutus, “rolled together,” from convolvere: con (together) + volvere (to roll).

mn.text: The signposts at the crossroads point every which way, and the directions twist around and back. Jamal gives up: the route is {convoluted}.

scene.alt: A dizzy man with a map stares at signposts pointing every which way.

head: word
clear or not?
you might hear
rows: hard to see into or understand
after.cap: From crystal clear to hopelessly tangled.

after.html: Explicit and implicit are opposites: explicit is said outright; implicit is suggested without being said. Implicit does not mean hidden on purpose. (In “implicit trust,” it has a second sense: complete and unquestioning.) And obscure has two senses: hard to understand (an obscure poem) and little known (an obscure village).

opts.s: The rules of the game were {explicit}: printed in large letters right on the inside of the box lid.
opts.why: Rules printed out plainly are stated outright: explicit.

items.q: Dad never said the cookies were for the party, but the message was ______ when he hid the jar on the top shelf. Which word fits?
items.why: The message was suggested by what Dad did, not said: implicit.

items.q: In “an obscure village that few maps show,” obscure means…
items.why: A village few maps show is little known. Obscure can also mean hard to understand, but not here.

items.q: True or false: implicit means hidden on purpose.
items.why: False. Implicit means suggested without being said. Nothing has to be hidden; it simply goes unspoken.

items.q: The Latin root luc in lucid and elucidate means…
items.why: Luc (from lux) means light: a lucid idea is clear as daylight, and to elucidate is to bring something into the light.

items.q: Type the word that means so twisted and complicated that it is hard to follow.
items.why: Convoluted comes from Latin for rolled together: twisted up in knots.
